speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking part in the debate this afternoon. However the treatises which have been read in the house in the past two days leads me to the belief that the government of the day looks on the House of Commons as the family vault, the doors of which are to be opened only once in a while. Last year on January 25 the doors were opened, and closed immediately upon the calling of an election. The vault opened again on May 16, and closed on August 7. At this time it has again been opened, and we have been privileged to hear the last wills and testaments of many cabinet ministers.
While I do not wish to be critical of any of them, there are some observations I should like to make. I know the ministers are working hard. The one who has just completed his speech has done a great deal of work in connection with the re-arming of Canada and the general cleaning up of the situation. For such work he deserves a great deal of credit. My point is this, that if the forty minute rule, which you, Mr. Speaker, so fairly interpreted the other day, is not to apply to ministers we might as well adopt the practice at Washington where members of congress simply hand in, without reading them, pamphlets running to three and four hundred pages, and they are printed in the record.
I think I was the victim who perhaps led to the adoption of the forty minute rule. Away back when a great many members now here were not in this house, four or five notorious bills came up. One was the Sun Life bill, which the privy council declared illegal. Another was the Bell Telephone bill, to cut a melon of $75,000,000 at the expense

of the taxpayers of Ontario. Another bill proposed to give away all the power in the Ottawa valley to the Sifton interests, and another was the Beauhamois bill. I opposed all these bills and they were talked out by the opposition on this side of the house, and our action saved the country hundreds of millions of dollars. The old rule was good enough from confederation down to the time when the rules were amended. It was hardly ever abused.
The first point I want to make here today is this: Why have we not national government in this country, a government representative of all the people? This is just a Liberal war. We come here and hear these statements read by one minister after the other, seeking to soothe the people into a false sense of security when we are not secure. I did not wait until the war broke out to preach rearmament. I preached it right along from the opposition benches during the whole time I was a member of the house. The more we have of these speeches by the ministers the more we realize that the government believe the pen is mightier than the sword. That was the view the isolationists took in the United States and the pacifists in Great Britain, and this government evidently believes in that same doctrine. When war broke out the British government sent six million leaflets to be dropped over Germany, thinking that by propaganda they could convert the German people to the British government's view, and the third day after war was declared ten million leaflets were dropped over Germany. They believed then that the pen was mightier than the sword. What the people of this country want to know is whether we are secure or not, instead of having all these speeches. Security is better than opulence. We know we are not secure.
I believe there is a call to-day for national government in Canada. I think it would be in the interests of the government itself and in the interests of our war effort. In a real democracy the opposition necessarily shares responsibility with the government. It is the alternative government.
Some hon. gentlemen opposite criticized the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White), but that gentleman has already shown his zeal in this war by wearing the king's uniform and serving as a company commander training the young recruits. The House of Commons is the only place where a soldier or a citizen can have his grievance remedied or where the man on the

The Address-Mr. Church
street can learn what the facts are and what are the policies of the government and those who oppose it.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply is a very able minister with a fine record in private business. I think I have known him as long as anybody in the house. He is a sincere and hard-working man. I knew him as an engineer when I was chairman of the Toronto harbour board, and I have been acquainted with the good work he has done. He has worked hard and well and I know his heart is in his work. I believe he has tried to do his duty. I do not know the whole story but I believe he has done his bit to the best of his ability, even though he supports the policies of the government and the way they administer the affairs of the country.
In Great Britain the Labour party under Mr. Lansbury opposed all measures of rearmament. From 1931 to 1935 the opposition was committed to pacifism, and pacifism was sweeping the country. In a by-election at East Fulham, in 1933, the issue was the pacifist issue, and the "peace and disarmament" candidate, Mr. J. C. Wilmot, turned a Conservative majority of 14,521 into a Labour majority of 4,840. Mr. Baldwin, commenting in 1936 with appalling candour on this colossal turnover, said:
Now supposing I had gone to the country (in 1935) and had said "Germany is rearming; we must rearm." Does anyone think that this pacific democracy of ours would have rallied to that cry? Not at that moment. I cannot think of anything which would have made the loss of the election, from my point of view, more certain.
Mr. Lansbury had long been the head of the Labour party, and you all know his pacifism-"not a dollar, not a man," and all that kind of thing. Then he lost the leadership of the party and Mr. Bevin and Mr. Morrison and Sir Stafford Cripps came to the forefront. Then there was the peace ballot in Great Britain and the general strike, the Independent Labour party under Mr. Keir Hardie, and the socialist league, all warning the government in no circumstances to go to war. Sir Stafford Cripps was a pure pacifist. In 1933, at Bristol, he said:
I think we ought to warn the government that in no circumstances will we go to war. There is only one way in which we can make that threat effective, and that is to call a general strike.
Last but not least there was the League of Nations Union, which has done more damage and done more to cause this war than almost any other agency.
What do we find to-day? We find the British government has formed a cabinet of all
parties and taken in a lot of pacifists. Mr. Herbert Morrison is a very energetic Minister of Supply, whose work is universally admitted to have been very valuable. He and Mr. Bevin have been more successful than any preceding minister in pursuading trade unionists to suspend their regulations and in securing an increased output of munitions. Nevertheless, until he was admitted to the ranks of the ministry, Mr. Morrison in the London county council, for instance, or its committees under his direction, abolished the celebration of empire day in the schools, decided not to sanction the maintenance of cadet corps or officers' training corps, refused to assist in military pageants or tattooes, declined the use of the schools for purposes of recruiting or drill, withdrew grants for scholarships to enable boys to become officers in the Royal Navy, denied permission to children in schools to attend lectures on the navy, banned in 1936 circulation in the schools of Earl Beatty's empire day message. Mr. Morrison himself said at Islington on March 22, 1935:
The Labour majority had to take into account that a large number of parents, and a growing body of public opinion, had a deep objection to the military training of the young.
The League of Nations Union was started in 1920 as a non-party organization to make the work of the league known and win popular support for it, but it gradually passed under the control of pacifists, cranks, socialists, cosmopolitans, with the result that from 1931 onward it became increasingly anti-government, deprecated recruiting, took a leading part in organizing the peace ballot of 1934-35, changed the mind of the Baldwin-MacDonald government and led the dictators to believe no matter what they did Britain would be neutral.
My point is this. Notwithstanding that France, when war broke out, had a socialist government, the United States a new deal government, Great Britain a Conservative government, and Canada a Liberal government; and notwithstanding the fact that in all these countries isolationism, pacifism and all that sort of thing had held sway for years, the British government stopped all that in Great Britain by forming a national government representative of all parties that rearmed after Munich and since the war united the nation. I am a strong supporter of the trade unionist movement and always have been, but I believe the government of the day in Great Britain did the right thing with respect to the trade unionists by calling in all parties -labour element and opposition, many of whom had helped cause the war-in order to present a united front to the enemy.
The Address-Mr. Church

Why does not this government do the same thing? That is the first point I raise in this debate. Why does not this government take the same action that the British government took, instead of having in office in Canada a purely Liberal party government run on party lines? Let us rather have a government representative of all the people from Halifax to Vancouver and put politics in cold storage until after the war. Such a government would have the united and loyal support of the whole country.
Secondly, I would ask where are we now in this war? We have now had almost fifteen months of war. We have seen Hitler capture, by diplomacy and fraud and the ferocity of his attacks, practically the whole of Europe except Russia and two little islands at the edge of Europe-Great Britain and Ireland. Where are we now? Are we secure? Are we secure enough? No, we are not. We are not going to be able to fight Hitler by books and pamphlets and orders in council and the reading of treatises and all that kind of thing. The defence of Canada will never be decided at Vancouver or Quebec or Halifax or Saint John; it is going to be decided in the battle of Britain. The battle of Britain is now on in the Mediterranean and other fronts, and if they fail over there all our home defence is at an end, and so is that of the United States.
I am very much dissatisfied in a great many ways with the work the government has done. First, they have given the House of Commons no information. I referred to that in 1938 and 1939 and in the two sessions this year. Mr. Chamberlain said in 1938 and 1939 that if the people are not given the facts, if they are given only so much as their rulers allow them to know, they are embarked on a course which is fraught with grave consequences for the future. That was proven to be true. Criticism is a tonic. It is good for the individual, it is good for the government. It stirs governments to action. If the criticism is founded on fact and not based on partisan objects it can do nothing but help; it can save the government from many pitfalls and mistakes, grave perils and dangers.
Now, the criticism regarding this war effort is justified. The opposition has a responsibility to the soldier and to the country to perform its duty when information is lacking. In such statements as we have had during the last three or four days there is a lack of information. There is also too much Hollywood ballyhoo about our publicity. In my opinion the bureau of public information should be wiped out altogether-it has been a centre of mischief ever since it was started- and the press instead should be given this

responsibility and these functions. How does it come about that to a very large extent only United States citizens-some of them newspaper correspondents-have been chosen to do this work? The bureau has a broadcast which they call " Facing the Facts." They are not facts at all. A great many of them are only half-truths. The speakers deal largely with opinions and are in the realm of doubt all the time. They forget all about Britain that has given the United States all the peace it has had so far.
In a democracy the opposition shares responsibility with the government. Its business is to criticize the government's policy, and if its views make a popular appeal the government is generally compelled to make revisions, by concessions, compromises, and so forth. Reading the handwriting on the wall often saves a government from its own friends.
The collapse of France was caused because the people were not given the facts, but were kept in the dark. But for the isolationism of Canada, long before the war began the dominions would have been invited to participate in a war plan. Canada should have been delighted to do so, but Canada was lukewarm and drifted. Canada was one of the chief objectors and isolationists before the war. At the outbreak of the war she was not prepared. As in 1812, she had to depend on Britain, on land and sea and in the air, for defence.
What the House of Commons and the people want to get is real information and the real picture. The picture which the minister has just disclosed is a very rosy one, but you cannot fight Hitler by explaining what you are going to do in 1943, 1944 and 1945. The government's attitude reminds me of the United States, where congress was shocked by the chairman of the war committee, Mr. Wiliam Knudsen, when he said that it would be 1944 before the United States could mobilize, train and equip an army or get a proper rearmament programme. We are in the same position.
In debate on March 24, 1938, when the government of the day put up member after member from Quebec and other centres to tell the country that not a dollar was to be spent ex-terri'torially, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said we would never send another expeditionary force overseas, that the danger to Canada was minor in degree and secondary in origin, and all that kind of thing, I took the position that we should have a survey made of all the large and small plants in Canada and that there should be a national register and national service. About the time of the Ethiopian campaign, in 1936 and 1937, I proposed an

The Address

Mr. Church
air scheme linked up with the Department of Labour, whereby the young people from our schools and high schools who were out of work and looking for jobs could enter the aeroplane industry, learn a trade, learn something about air training, take some drill, receive pocket money, food, clothing and lodging, so that at the end of from three to five years they would be available either as pilots or in those branches of industry which are now doing from coast to coast the key work which the minister has so ably set forth.
What the country wants to know is when we shall have deliveries of shells and bombers and aeroplanes and aeroplane engines and guns and rifles,

all that sort of thing. I have seen soldiers out on parade along the streets, and they have not got any of this equipment. In the debate last year I put forward the constructive idea that Canada should find a way of making possible the impossible. In other words, where there are no barracks or implements of war we should do as we did before, namely, take other public buildings. If men have no uniforms, let them train without uniforms. If they have no rifles, machine guns or other modern implements of warfare, then they should do what has been done in France and Great Britain, namely use dummies until the real weapons can be obtained. Instead of allowing these men to drift around with nothing to do, they should be given the proper training immediately. Toronto is the main recruiting district in Canada, and I do not know what is going to be done there, or elsewhere. The men want to get overseas. This is not the way to fight Hitler. The government should wake up. We shall never beat Hitler and win this war if we go on the way we are going now. As I said in 1938, it takes two years to train a man, and two years to get munitions, and then six months afterwards for the soldier to learn how to use the armaments with which he is then provided.
As I have said, France fell because she was denied the simple truth about the way things were going. After all the items of news which we have had, I doubt if we could produce a white book or paper about our relations with the continent and with the United States or with Britain since the war began. I have seen nothing of the kind. The house has not been given the facts. Sir Robert Borden used to say that when he had a secret he wanted to keep he should tell it to his cabinet. When the present Prime Minister has a secret he wants to keep, he seems to tell it to a do-nothing Canada-United States defence committee, or to fifty United States
newspaper editors who come over here and then go back to their own country and publish these secrets in United States newspapers, over the head of the House of Commons, the members of which do not know the secrets, and over the heads of the people who have the right to know what is going on and how their money is -being spent. The dictators knew all these so-called secrets long ago.
The revelations of the strength and skill of the German army and the way they smashed through the low countries and Scandinavia have shocked this country and awakened the United States. But where are we now? In the olden days battles lasted only a day or two. With the increase of population and the advent of mechanized equipment, battles nowadays go on for one, two, three and four years. Germany to-day is headed by a chancellor whom the people worship and idolize. We thought that he could be easily defeated and that, for that reason, war would never come. But what has actually happened? In the last great war Germany kept the whole civilized world at bay for four and a half years, notwithstanding that at that time we had on our side Italy, Russia, the United States and Japan. Now Italy and Japan at any rate are against us-one is fighting against us and the other is a potential enemy-all on account of the appeasement policy that had been pursued. We have lost Japan, our old and faithful ally who looked after the Pacific, Australia, New Zealand and the empire in the east. She was driven out of the Anglo-Japanese alliance to appease America. The same with Italy. These two countries should never have gone against us. It was a fatal mistake to lose two old friends and loyal allies.
You cannot beat Hitler with any tower of babel such as we have, as represented in so many agencies including our information bureau, the typewriter and quires of foolscap, and the radio, and government by order in council. History is being gloriously rewritten by our men on land and sea and in the air and we should see to it that they are given proper equipment. Let me refer the house to the stirring words of Mr. Churchill, after the collapse of France, on the duty to inform the public and tell them the truth, no matter how bad.
During this time of w,ar great powers are entrusted to executive governments. Nevertheless we exercise them under the constant supervision of parliament and with a wide measure of free debate. We have a stern and resolute House of Commons which is not likely at all to flag or weaken in the conflict upon which we entered unanimously. And I do not doubt that it is the House of Commons which will
The Address

Mr. Church

not hesitate if emergency requires it to approve and enforce all measures necessary for the safety of the state.
During the last 250 years the British parliament has fought several great and long European wars with unwearied zeal and tenacity, and carried them all to a successful conclusion. In this war they are fighting not only for themselves but for parliamentary institutions wherever they have been set up. In our country public men are proud to be the servants of the people. They would be ashamed to be their masters. The ministers of the crown feel themselves strengthened by having at their side this House of Commons and House of Lords, sitting with great regularity and active as a continual stimulus to their activities.
Of course it is quite true that there is often severe criticism of the government in the two houses. We do not resent well-meant criticism from any man who wishes to win the war; we do not even shrink from unfair criticism, though that is most dangerous. On the contrary, we take it constantly to heart and seek to profit by it.
Criticism in the body politic is like pain in the human body. It is unpleasant, but where would the body be without it? No health or sensibility would be possible without the continued correctives and warnings of pain.
It is in this fear of criticism that the nazi and bolshevik dictators run their greatest risk. They silence all criticism by the concentration camp, the rubber truncheon or the firing party. The men at the top must very often be fed only with facts which are palatable to them. Scandals, corruption and shortcomings are not exposed, because there are no independent voices. Instead of being exposed, they continue to fester behind the pompous frontage of the state.
The men at the top may be very fierce and powerful, but their ears are deaf. Their fingers are numb. They cannot feel their feet as they move forward in the fog and darkness of the immeasurable and the unknown.
One of the things that this war is going to prove is whether in modern times the full strength of nations can be realized under totalitarian systems working through an ogpu or a gestapo.
I believe the time has come when the press censorship in Canada should be abolished entirely and we should go back to the good old British system, leaving the responsibility for censorship as largely as possible to the voluntary effort of the press. This is what Britain is doing. There are one or two press censors there who supervise things but the press is left largely alone. In my opinion it would be far better for the Canadian people, and it would make for the dissemination of more reliable information, if that policy were followed in this country. After all, the press has certain duties to the public. It is the medium through which the government of the day can impart information to the people, and I submit that it should not be trammelled, but should be let tell the truth. Truth is [DOT]the first victim of this war, and self-respect is the victim of neutrality.

In my opinion the National Resources Mobilization Act should be repealed altogether. It has proved a failure. If the same amount of money that has been expended under it had been devoted to a voluntary system of recruiting there would be nearly one million men under arms in Canada to-day instead of the comparatively small force which we have under this complicated and useless method, headed by civilians who know nothing of war. The system now in force has been weighed in the balance and found wanting. It is headed by civilians and there is altogether too much red tape, delay and cumbersome procedure about it. They seem to think that we can fight Hitler in that way, but they will have a rude awakening. In the last war we did not have so many ministers directing our defences as we have to-day. We have good men for militia, air, and the navy. At the present time there is no system of check and balance and in consequence there is continuous friction among the services, and waste and duplication. The system should be abolished and we should go back ,to the old method. There is something of the Alice in Wonderland way in the conducting of our war effort. They seem to think that what they have done is simply wonderful, but it is not getting men over to fight Hitler and help in the battle of Britain.
May I say a word now with regard to the Rowell commission-I say Rowell commission because in my opinion it should be so designated. Chief Justice Rowell was the original chairman of the commission, and the other members have not the learning and ability or the wide knowledge of constitutional questions, or the judgment, that the original chairman had. However, the question I should like to ask is this: Why is the report of the commission to be considered at this stage? The report was relegated to the archives last session-earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust, in sure hope that it would not be resurrected. Why is it being revived now in the darkest hour of the war? Why not postpone consideration of it until after the war? It is a red herring dragged across the track now to hinder our war effort.
It seems to me that the report of the Rowell commission does not tackle the main question that confronts the people of Canada to-day, namely, overgovernment and overtaxation. We should never have had any provincial legislatures; they are duplicate municipal systems. They were created by the fathers of confederation for political and not for economic purposes. We want a British North America Act for the living and not for the dead. The report, I repeat, does not

The Address-Mr. Church
deal with the main, question as to the elimination of provincial legislatures. If the provisions of the report are adopted it will simply mean that the province of Ontario will become the hewer of wood and the drawer of water for the rest of the confederation.
We have four ministers from the province of Ontario and not one of them is in the house this afternoon. We have heard from a young minister representing an Ontario constituency. He spoke yesterday. I have not the pleasure of his acquaintance, though I have no doubt he is very much respected in the maritime provinces. He now represents the city of Kingston in this house. I would impress upon these ministers representing the province of Ontario that the province is being overtaxed, and is the forgotten province of confederation. Under the Municipal Assistance Act the province of Quebec has been given many concessions in relief legislation and votes. Many institutions have been provided, parks and sidewalks and other purely municipal services, out of federal funds, while Ontario has received nothing, and no such favours in relief votes. It seems to me that the report, while undoubtedly satisfactory from the point of view of the prairie provinces, will shake the very foundations of confederation if it is carried into effect. From the very start I have strenuously opposed the way in which the dominion and provinces have encroached upon the rights of the municipalities and robbed them of their revenues. Federal power now is at its lowest ebb since confederation. One has only to mention income tax. There are some good features in the report, but I submit that it can be laid over until after the war is won, because if Hitler wins it will not matter whether the report is adopted or not. After the war the wreckage will be so great there will be nothing to salvage in Canada.
There are many matters that one might discuss in this debate. It seems to me that the time has come when we should get rid of the dummy for the nazi ventriloquist, the Petain French embassy in Canada. A great British newspaper said recently:
We publish a note of Lord Milner's on the war crisis of March, 1918. In it will be seen how Marshal Petain had to be pushed and pulled along by Clemenceau and Foch, and in the latter's war book it is described how, later in 1918, Petain proposed surrender. It does not appear that he actually used the word at Doullens in the presence of the British, but speaking to the French he predicted the surrender of Marshal Haig within a month of the Doullens gathering.	Surrender would
appear to be part of his make-up. Another side of his character is seen in his seeking to throw blame on others.	He and General
Weygand were in charge of the French army until 1935, for Marshal Petain was inspector-general of the French military forces from 1922 to 1931, and he was war minister in 1934. General Weygand was the head of the French general staff, that is head of the army, from 1931 to 1935. These generals, therefore, must not take the line that they have no responsibility for French military plans and training or for the failure of both. Between them they had control from the vital year 1922 to 1935, the lessons of modern mechanization had been learned by others. General de Gaulle published his great book, Vers VArmes de Metier, in 1934. General Weygand and Marshal Petain paid no attention to it, but Hitler reorganized his whole army in accordance with its precepts, and his generals derived their plans for the battle of France very largely from the principles there laid down. One more point. In his radio apologia to the French for his surrender to Germany, Marshal Petain said that France had too few allies and too few children. The marshal's treatment of French allies will certainly not add to the number of those seeking "alliance with France, and in regard to too few children, Marshal Petain himself only married when he was sixty-four and has none at all. He probably forgot this when he spoke, as indeed he now forgets everything. Most of his day is spent asleep, and while his interlocutors are actually talking to him he forgets who they are and asks their names. A perfect tool for the enemies of his country; a piteous end for a brave soldier.
I am sorry for the great tragedy to glorious France, our immortal ally of old. I am sorry for the way in which Petain acted; he was a great general. I am very sorry for the glorious French people because we all recognize their bravery, devotion and love of freedom. They are now under the heel of the invader and with the cold of winter coming on we see the result of their work. We should close up the Petain mission and like England recognize the French provincial government.
We should also have some understanding regarding some of the other nations.
When Mr. Churchill speaks in the House of Commons he is listened to by the wide world. One reason why he stands above others is that he has no "ghost" or anonymous helper writing out his utterances for him, as is the case with so many public men in other countries. Mr. Churchill's speeches are his own, and they rank high in the annals of British oratory, like the one in which he told the House of Commons two or three weeks ago:
It has come to us to stand alone at the breach and face the worst that the tyrant's might and enmity can do. Bearing ourselves humbly before God, but conscious that we serve an unfolding purpose, we are ready to defend our native land against the invasion by which it is threatened. We are fighting by ourselves alone. But we are not fighting for ourselves alone . . .
The Address-Mr. Church

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after having listened to this debate for the past several days I feel it my duty, as the representative of a rural constituency, to say a few words with regard to the problem which we face in Ontario, and more particularly in that part of the province from which I come.
Before doing so, however, I should like to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Both these hon. gentlemen did credit to themselves as well as to the constituencies they represent. I should like also to add a word of appreciation for the clear manner in

The Address-Mr. Rickard
which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) presented Canada's war effort to this house and told us what would be expected of us as Canadians. I should like also to congratulate the various ministers who have spoken, upon the way in which they have handled the situation and the work they have done. They have shown that they know their jobs and understand what it is all about. To my mind they have presented to the house and to the country a clear picture of what is being done in connection with our part in this war.
Some criticism has come from the press and other sources because the government has not divulged all the secrets of this war effort. Those of us who read the Globe and Mail are perhaps more familiar with these statements, because there from time to time we have seen comments that nothing has been done, that we have not been told half the story, and so on. I am one of those who believe that agitations of this kind do more harm than good as far as our war effort is concerned. We all know that certain matters cannot be made public. We also know that the empire is engaged in a mortal struggle, and we are convinced that we are fighting for the right. Because of this the Canadian people are prepared to make unlimited sacrifices. What is more, they want to do anything they can to help win this war. Victory will come only after a long, bitter struggle, and there will be a time and place for all to help.
My purpose in taking part in this debate is not particularly to discuss Canada's war effort, which already has been debated at some length, but rather to give this house in my humble way some idea of the conditions facing the man on the land in this province of Ontario. The other evening the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) lamented the condition of the western wheat grower. He criticized some portions of the government's policy, and offered certain suggestions which he thought would remedy the situation as far as the west was concerned. But he did not give the government any praise for anything the government had done in connection with markets, which I thought he might have done if he had desired to be fair.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Tell us what they have done.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Just a moment. As a
farmer I know I have received more for my produce since this government came to office than I received under the previous government. After 1930 I well remember selling hogs for 3i cents a pound and less, and cattle at 4 and 41 cents a pound; cheese
went down to 10 cents a pound, and so on.
I am not arguing that we are getting enough for our produce to-day, but I do say that since this government came into power and made a trade treaty with the United States, which permitted us to ship our surplus cattle to that market, many thousands of dollars have been placed in the pockets of the Canadian farmers. More than that, I believe that same trade treaty has had a good effect in bringing about a closer relationship between Canada and the United States which is proving veiy helpful as far as our war effort is concerned.
To-day governments, both provincial and federal, are spending thousands of dollars in trying to educate our young men and women to stay on the farms. Only recently, there were held in every province of the dominion judging competitions, the winners of which were given free trips to Ottawa in order to see the highlights of this capital city; they were here only a week or so ago. Boys from Durham county won two dominionwide contests, in seed judging and potato judging, and were only six points from winning a third. Ours was the only county in the country ro win two prizes. But now, after we have done a great deal to keep our young people on the farms, industry comes along and takes every available man. It seems to be well recognized that farm boys make the very best men in industry; of course they are good men anywhere. As I say, I am not arguing that the farmer is getting his fair share, or that the prices of the commodities which he has to sell are nearly high enough, but I do say that we are better off now than we were under the previous administration.
There is no class of people under the sun more willing to do what they can for Canada's war effort than the farmers. Wherever possible they have contributed to the war loans. Without complaint they have allowed their sons to leave the farms for their thirty-day training. They and their wives and families have interested themselves in the work of the Red Cross and other organizations which will help win this war, but they expect a fair and decent return for their labour, just as industry, just as the business man and just as the labouring man expect a fair return.
That brings me to the labour problem, which is a very important question in Ontario. With present prices of farm commodities it is impossible for the farmers to compete with industry as far as wages are concerned. I am not opposed to labour getting everything it can, because I believe that labour has been kept down too long.
The Address-Mr. Rickard

But to-day hundreds of farmers in Ontario are leaving their farms and going to work in the shops because in two weeks they can earn more money there than they can make on a farm in three or four months. Perhaps we have overproduced. It is said that we have a surplus of eight hundred million bushels of wheat; we have been persuading Great Britain to take more of our pork, and we may have too much butter for home consumption. I should like, however, to sound a warning. I believe that if the war continues for another two or three years we may find that we have not enough of these commodities to meet the demand.
As I said before, many farmers are leaving the land to work in the factories. Many others told me they were just going to plough what land they could sow, take off and sell the crop and let the rest go. Other farmers to my knowledge are getting up early in the morning, doing their chores before daylight, driving to town and working in factories all day, then coming back and doing their chores again at night. In my opinion this sort of thing cannot continue. If anything can be done for the farmer in Ontario or in any other part of eastern Canada, or for the farmer in western Canada, it should be done now, before our whole system is upset.
In his speech delivered a few days ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) told us what we could sell to Great Britain in the coming year, and described in detail the agreement between Great Britain and Canada. He said that we may sell wheat and dairy products. In the latter group we must include cheese, and of that commodity we are to sell all we can produce, at a price of 14.4 cents a pound to the producer. We are to sell bacon and other cured meats, canned and fresh fish, poultry, eggs, canned fruits and vegetables-but practically no fresh fruits. As a fruit grower it is natural that I should be disappointed in Great Britain's decision not to take our apples. If, however, that decision has been made, we shall have to make the best of our home market.
Great Britain is willing to take some $12,000,000 worth of fish from the maritime provinces, and with that provision I am pleased. As farmers we are not satisfied with the price of bacon set by the British government, but if it is a price which permits the fanner to know exactly *what he is going to get the year round, the situation may not be too bad. To-day the farmer in Ontario should receive at least $8.50 per hundredweight, live weight, at his bam, if he is going to get any return on his expenditure. The price of

farm produce to-day is altogether too low, when compared with what the farmer has to pay. All kinds of implements of production have increased in price. Lumber, building materials, wire fencing, hardware of all kinds, boots and shoes and practically all the necessities of life have advanced in price at least to some degree. Some have not advanced very much, but have done so sufficiently to make the difference between profit and loss to the farmer. Hundreds of farmers are to-day making only a bare living on the land, and every assistance is necessary if they are to keep going, and do their best to help in Canada's war effort.
I do impress upon the government the necessity of seriously considering the condition in which the farmers of eastern Canada as well as those in the west find themselves. Let us all try to work together, and do something to help the farmer in his war effort. Let us work toward the building of a greater Canada.
On motion of Mr. Ilsley the debate was adjourned.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, November 21, 1940.
